name: GBL

tolerance.full: within several days of continuous use

addictionPotential: Highly physically and moderately to highly psychologically addictive
toxicities: GBL is identified as a GHB prodrug, and combining GABAergic depressants with opioids, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, gabapentinoids, thienodiazepines or alcohol is warned against as potentially causing a fatal overdose. A stimulant comedown is specifically warned about, as it can leave a depressant effect overwhelming the user and causing respiratory arrest.
effectsSummary: The effect is extremely dose-dependent and varies greatly from individual to individual. It also depends on the purity of the substance. The spectrum of effects ranges from euphoria, relaxation, disinhibition, intensification of perception, urge to talk (babble flash), slight dizziness and drowsiness to deep (coma-like) sleep or unconsciousness.
dosageRemark: The archived oral table lists threshold 0.3 mL, light 0.3-0.9 mL, moderate 0.9-1.5 mL, strong 1.5-3 mL (the page warns >2 mL may induce deep sleep), heavy 3 mL+; total 1-2 h, onset 3-10 min, comeup 5-15 min, peak 30-45 min, offset 15-30 min and afterglow 1-3 h. Educational user/resource compilation, not a recommendation. GBL is converted in the body to GHB and 1 mL GBL is equivalent to 1.66 g sodium GHB; liquids of unknown concentration introduce uncertainty.
generalRisks: GBL is converted to GHB in the body. FreeODwiki warns strong sedation and potentially fatal overdose when combined with other depressants; it says doses above 2 mL may induce deep sleep and cautions against measuring errors. The higher the dose, the more likely nausea, vomiting and dizziness will occur. Headaches, confusion, breathing difficulties, cardiac arrhythmias, impaired balance and memory can occur at very high doses, as can uncontrollable muscle twitching, which is easily mistaken for epilepsy but can also progress into epileptic seizures. The danger of an unintentional overdose is very high with GBL - even if it is not mixed. Signs of a GBL overdose are severe drowsiness followed by several hours of deep sleep that cannot be disturbed or can only be disturbed with difficulty (sometimes interrupted by short periods of wakefulness, the standing man symptom), and the risk of respiratory arrest and death. One of the reasons is that the dose cannot be measured accurately enough, because the concentration of GBL differs greatly from batch to batch and the product is often diluted to unknown concentrations. With regular use, tolerance develops quickly and withdrawal symptoms may occur.
longtermRisks: Regular use of GBL can lead to sleep disorders, anxiety and tremors; there is a risk of dependence with psychological and physical symptoms. In the case of chronic high-dose consumption (several doses daily), severe physical withdrawal symptoms such as sweating, muscle cramps or epileptic seizures occur upon discontinuation.
saferUse: Combining GBL or GHB with other depressants is strongly advised against, especially at moderate to heavy doses, because of the risk of a fatal overdose.
The archive warns prepared liquid concentration may be unknown; it distinguishes GBL volume from GHB mass and advises cross-checking its educational user/resource dose data.
summary: A pro-drug to GHB whose rapid absorption leads it to have a faster onset and shorter duration. Used in a similar manner to GHB, as a less-toxic alternative to alcohol. Consume slowly instead of as a "shot" to hugely improve safety and reduce overdose risk.
